client: I've been feeling really anxious about this family reunion coming up next month, and honestly it's been keeping me up at night. My cousin has this habit of making these cutting remarks about my job in front of everyone, and I just dread having to sit there and take it while the whole family watches. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, because at the end of the day the reunion is still happening and my cousin isn't going to magically become a different person.
therapist: It sounds like this situation is carrying a real weight for you — the dread of being publicly embarrassed, combined with feeling like there's no way out, can be genuinely exhausting, especially when it's disrupting your sleep. You're right that we can't change your cousin, but what we *can* explore is how you relate to those moments — the thoughts that run through your mind when the remarks happen, and whether there are ways to feel less at their mercy. What tends to go through your head in those moments when your cousin makes a comment — what's the story you find yourself telling yourself about what it means?

client: Honestly, in those moments I think something like "everyone here agrees with what she's saying" and "they all think I'm a failure too, they're just too polite to say it out loud." It's like her words become this confirmation of something I already secretly worry about — that I haven't done enough with my life compared to everyone else in the family. And then I just kind of shut down and go quiet, which probably makes it look like I agree with her, which makes everything feel even worse.
therapist: That thought — "everyone secretly agrees with her" — is doing a lot of heavy lifting in those moments, and it sounds like it lands with a quiet but deep sting, almost like your cousin is just giving voice to a fear you already carry. In CBT we'd call that a kind of mind-reading, where our anxious mind fills in the silence of others with our worst fears rather than actual evidence. I'm curious — if you were to look for real evidence, what do you actually *know* about how the other family members view your life and your choices?

client: I mean, my aunt did tell me last Thanksgiving that she thought it was brave that I'd taken a less conventional path, and my brother has never once made me feel bad about where I am. But here's the thing — in the moment when my cousin is talking, those examples just completely vanish from my mind, like they don't even exist. I guess I can see what you're pointing at with the mind-reading thing, but I'm not sure knowing that will actually help me hold onto those other voices when I'm sitting right there at the table feeling humiliated.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already identify those counter-examples — your aunt's words, your brother's consistent support — because that tells us the evidence *exists*, it just gets drowned out in the heat of the moment. This is actually something we can prepare for deliberately, almost like building a mental "rescue kit" — a specific phrase or image you rehearse beforehand so it's already primed and ready when the anxiety tries to erase everything else. What do you think it would feel like to walk into that reunion having already decided on one clear, grounding thought to hold onto when your cousin speaks?

client: I want to say it would feel better, but honestly my first reaction is skepticism — like, can a prepared phrase really hold up against the actual rush of embarrassment in that moment? It sounds good in theory, but I've told myself things before going into stressful situations and then completely forgotten them the second things got uncomfortable. I guess I'm worried this is one of those things that works on paper but falls apart when real feelings are involved.
therapist: Your skepticism is really valid, and it actually shows good self-awareness — you've tried to coach yourself before and watched it fall apart under pressure, so trusting this approach takes a leap of faith you haven't seen pay off yet. The difference we'd want to build here isn't just a phrase you *tell* yourself, but a practiced response that's been rehearsed enough times that it becomes almost automatic — more like a reflex than a reminder. Have you ever had an experience, even outside of family situations, where something you'd practiced or prepared for actually *did* hold up when things got hard?

client: Actually, yeah — I used to get really bad nerves before presentations at work, and I did this thing where I practiced out loud so many times that eventually my mouth just kind of knew what to do even when my brain was panicking. So I guess there is something to the repetition idea, I'll give you that. But a work presentation feels different from a family dinner because at work I had control over the whole thing, and with my cousin I have no idea when she's going to say something or what it's going to be.
therapist: That's a really important connection you just made — your nervous system actually *does* know how to use repetition to build steadiness under pressure, and that's not a small thing. You're right that the unpredictability with your cousin is a real difference, but what we'd be rehearsing isn't a script for what *she* says — it's your internal response to the rush of embarrassment itself, so it's ready no matter when or how it arrives. What do you think that internal anchor might need to feel like for you — something that helps you remember who you are beyond that moment, rather than trying to argue back against her words?

client: I think it would need to feel less like a logical argument and more like something that just... steadies me, almost like a hand on my shoulder. Maybe something connected to the fact that I actually know my own reasons for the choices I've made, even if I can't explain them to my cousin in that moment. But I'm realizing as I say that, that I don't feel very connected to that sense of self-assurance most of the time, so I'm not sure I can just summon it on demand at a family dinner.
therapist: What you just described — that image of a hand on your shoulder, grounded in *your own* reasons for your choices — is actually quite profound, and it suggests you have more self-knowledge than you're giving yourself credit for. The fact that you don't feel connected to that assurance most of the time is really worth sitting with, because it points to something deeper we could work on together beyond just the reunion — building that relationship with yourself so it's there when you need it, not just something you're scrambling to find under pressure. What do you think gets in the way of you feeling connected to your own sense of self most often in your day-to-day life?

client: Honestly, I think a big part of it is that I spend a lot of time alone, and when you're alone with your thoughts too much, the critical voice gets really loud without anything to balance it out. I don't have many people I feel close enough to that I can just call and say "hey, I'm doubting myself today" — so that self-assurance doesn't really get reinforced from the outside either. It's kind of a lonely loop, and I'm not sure how to break into it.
therapist: What you're describing has a quiet, heavy kind of ache to it — not a crisis, but a slow drain, where the critical voice fills the silence because there aren't enough other voices to offer a different perspective. It's a really honest and important thing to name, because it means the work isn't just about surviving the reunion — it's about gradually building more moments where your sense of self gets reflected back to you in a warmer, truer way. I'm wondering — are there any small, low-stakes connections in your life right now, even ones that feel incomplete or imperfect, that might hold a seed of that kind of nourishment?

client: There's this one coworker I eat lunch with sometimes, and it's usually pretty surface-level stuff, but occasionally we have these moments where it feels like she actually gets me. I've thought about trying to deepen that friendship but then I talk myself out of it because I worry about coming on too strong or being too much for people. I guess that's another version of the same thing — assuming the worst about how I'll be received before anything has even happened.
therapist: You just made a really significant connection on your own — that the same mind-reading pattern that haunts you at the family dinner is also quietly closing doors in your everyday life, including with someone who has already shown you she *can* get you. There's something worth holding onto in the fact that those moments of genuine connection have already happened with her, which means the foundation isn't something you'd have to build from scratch. What do you think it might look like to take one small step toward her — something that feels like deepening without feeling like too much?

client: Maybe the next time we have one of those real moments at lunch, I could just... let it land instead of immediately deflecting with a joke or changing the subject, and maybe say something honest back instead of keeping it surface-level. But even as I say that, I notice I'm already thinking about how awkward it might feel, or what if she doesn't respond the way I'm hoping and then lunch becomes weird forever. I guess the stakes feel high even when I know logically they probably aren't.
therapist: There's something really tender and hopeful in what you just described — choosing to let a real moment land instead of deflecting is actually a quiet act of courage, even if it doesn't look dramatic from the outside. And it's so human that your mind immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario, but notice that the catastrophe you're imagining — "lunch becomes weird forever" — is another version of that same pattern of filling in the unknown with your fears rather than evidence. What do you think she's actually shown you so far, in those moments where she's gotten you, about how she tends to handle realness?

client: When I actually think about it, she's the one who usually goes a little deeper first — she's mentioned things about her own family being complicated, and she didn't seem to need me to fix it or respond perfectly, she just seemed to want to be heard. So I guess she has shown me that she can handle something real without it becoming a big deal. It's just that knowing that in my head and actually trusting it in the moment feel like two completely different things to me.
therapist: There's something quietly significant in what you just noticed — she's already *shown* you who she is in those moments, and the evidence is actually on the side of safety, not danger. That gap you're naming, between knowing something and being able to trust it in your body in the moment, is really at the heart of a lot of what we've been exploring today — and it's not a flaw, it's just where the deeper work lives. I'm wondering, given everything you've reflected on today, what feels like the most alive thread to keep pulling on — the reunion, this friendship, or that quieter question of how you build a more consistent relationship with your own sense of worth?
